title: Different roads
hook: by different means we reach the same end: sometimes mercy softens an enemy, sometimes courage (Essays 1.1)

segments.voice: Yesterday, the runaway horse: Montaigne's idle mind bolting, and his pen following it. Your line was the runaway horse. Where did yours run, and did you write it down? Day one thousand one hundred forty-eight.

Same fight, same parent, two different kids. One cries and says sorry, and the parent melts. The other stands there, chin up, and says, I did it, and I'd do it again, and somehow the parent melts for that one too. It happens at kitchen tables. Montaigne opens the whole book of Essays with it, the very first chapter, though his examples are a good deal bloodier: a conqueror at the gates of a town, and the question of what makes him stop.
screen: `ONE SAYS SORRY.` → `ONE STANDS FIRM.` → `BOTH ARE FORGIVEN.`

segments.voice: First, the usual road. The title says it: by different means we arrive at the same end. When someone we've wronged has us in their power, Montaigne says, the common way to soften them is to give in and move them to pity. Second, the other road. Sometimes the opposite works: courage and steadiness. His first story is a prince at the sack of a town. The people, the women and the children, throw themselves at his feet, and he isn't moved. Then he sees three gentlemen holding their ground against his whole army with astonishing boldness, and that is what stops his anger. He spares them, and then the town. Third, the surprise in the middle. Montaigne turns it on himself. He says he'd be the one swayed by pity, and more easily by pity than by admiration, though he knows the Stoics counted pity a fault. So the essay isn't a rule. It's two people, two roads, two different hearts. Fourth, the line that sends the whole book on its way. Man, he writes, is a marvelously vain, varied, and wavering thing; it's hard to build any steady judgment on him. A big claim for a first chapter. The essays after it keep trying to catch that wavering thing. And it fits our week. A village content at home. True words without polish. A Tao close. A tower, painted beams, a runaway horse. Different roads into the same quiet work. Close to home, the essay suggests that an approach that failed with one person might be the wrong road, not the wrong goal.
screen: `THE USUAL ROAD: PITY.` · `THE OTHER ROAD: COURAGE.` · `MONTAIGNE, MOVED BY PITY.` · `A WAVERING THING.` · then, large: `DIFFERENT ROADS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: try a different approach once. Sit and let the breath find its own way for a few rounds. Then bring to mind one place you keep taking the same road and getting the same result. A conversation with a teenager. A habit you keep trying to quit. A coworker who won't budge. What's the road you always take? Soft, or firm? Talking, or waiting? Now picture the other road, just once, and see where it might go. Rest there. The bell holds the time.
Different roads. Montaigne's first essay: by different means we reach the same end; sometimes pity softens a conqueror, sometimes courage does. Today's word.
Your line: different roads. Today, with one stuck situation, take the road you usually don't, and notice what happens. Day one thousand one hundred forty-eight.

howItsDone: Some readers of Montaigne take the first chapter of the Essays as a key to the whole book: people are too varied for one rule, so the same end can be reached by opposite means.

match.prompt: Montaigne's first essay: tap the pairs.
pairs: give in and move them to pity
held their ground and stopped his anger

myth: Montaigne says only pity can soften a conqueror
the essay's point is the opposite: by different means, pity or courage, we reach the same end.
Montaigne says he himself is more easily moved by pity
more by pity than by admiration, though he notes the Stoics counted pity a fault.
the prince in the story spared the town because the people begged
their pleas didn't move him; the courage of three gentlemen did.

fork.setup: you're the prince at the sack of the town. the people beg at your feet. then you see three men standing firm against your army. what moves you?
fork.reveal: in Montaigne's story the pleas didn't move him, but the boldness of the three gentlemen stopped his anger, and he spared them and then the town.

original.script: par divers moyens on arrive à pareille fin
original.say: par dee-VAIR mwah-YAN on ah-REEV ah pah-RAY FAN
original.note: French: by different means we arrive at the same end, the title of Montaigne's first essay.

trapdoor: what you thought: different roads means there's more than one way to do things.
what it means: people are moved by opposite things, pity or courage, so no single approach always works.
what a scholar hears: the first essay ends on man as a vain, varied, wavering subject, a line some readers take as the theme of the whole book.

sources.ref: Essays 1.1, By diverse means we arrive at the same end (submission or courage may soften a conqueror; the prince at the sack of a town spared it for three gentlemen's boldness; Montaigne more moved by pity; man a vain, diverse and wavering subject)

notes: Week-end day: looks back at days 1142–1147 by title. Also marks the opening of the Essays (1.1).
The prince is Edward, Prince of Wales, at Limoges in Montaigne's telling; the script leaves the name out to avoid an unchecked historical claim. A scholar may add it back.
Original is the French title of 1.1, 'Par divers moyens on arrive à pareille fin'; confirm spelling and pronunciation guide.

Editor: varied the hook opening away from day 1143's 'Two notes...'; smoothed the garbled week-recap line; 'weakness' to 'fault' for Montaigne's 'passion vicieuse'; varied the stock 'on an ordinary Tuesday' turn.
